**How the 'red flag law' works

Even though an officer in Indiana can take firearms from people deemed to be dangerous, state law still places limitations on that power of warrantless seizure.

After the seizure, the officer is required to submit a written statement to the court describing why the person is considered dangerous. If a judge finds that probable cause exists, the law enforcement agency can retain custody of the guns.

If not, the firearms are to be returned.

Because a judge reviews the seizures within 14 days and individuals have the opportunity to make their case in a court hearing, the law has proved relatively uncontroversial, Banks said.

A couple of other restrictions, which are often emphasized by gun-rights advocates during national debates, are also included in the language.

Officers aren't granted warrantless search and seizure power if a warrant is otherwise necessary.

Also, just because an individual has been released from a mental health facility or has a mental illness is not itself a precursor to having guns confiscated by police.

In Indianapolis, police officers will confiscate weapons when responding to scenes where someone is experiencing a mental health crisis.**
